# Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) {#sec-ancova}

```{r}
# Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

set.seed(538)

fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, digits = 3, format = "f"))
# For inline math: gives "< 0.001" or "= 0.035", so write $p `r fmt_p_eq(x)`$
fmt_p_eq <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< 0.001", paste("=", formatC(p, digits = 3, format = "f")))

# ANOVA table in the book's style: R's row labels, blank F and p on the Residuals row
anova_kable <- function(fit, caption = NULL) {
  broom::tidy(fit) |>
    mutate(
      sumsq     = round(sumsq, 2),
      meansq    = round(meansq, 2),
      statistic = ifelse(is.na(statistic), "", formatC(statistic, digits = 2, format = "f")),
      p.value   = ifelse(is.na(p.value), "", fmt_p(p.value))
    ) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Source", "df", "SS", "MS", "F", "p"),
                 align = "lrrrrr", caption = caption)
}
```

We've now covered regression (@sec-regression) and ANOVA (Chapters [-@sec-anova] and [-@sec-factorial-anova]). This chapter merges them:

$$\text{Regression} + \text{ANOVA} = \text{ANCOVA}$$

The last chapter compared macroinvertebrate species count across two discrete Pollution categories, present or absent, and two Flow categories, low or high. But suppose you measured each channel's pollution concentration instead of labeling it present or absent.

-   Does Flow's effect on species count still depend on pollution once pollution is treated as a continuous measurement instead of two groups? *(covariate: pollution concentration; factor: flow rate)*

-   Is the relationship between PFAS exposure and lifetime cancer incidence the same in low-income and high-income American populations? *(covariate: PFAS exposure; factor: income level)*

In each question, a continuous variable is related to the outcome, and a categorical variable splits the observations into groups.

The first question points to a limitation of the last chapter. "Pollution: present or absent" simplifies a continuous measurement, a concentration in parts per billion. Sorting continuous measurements into "high" and "low" buckets throws away the information a covariate needs, which is how much more polluted a channel is, not just whether it is polluted. Whenever you have the measured values, analyze them as a continuous covariate instead of forcing them into groups first. With a categorical factor still in the design, that analysis is ANCOVA. With no categorical factor left, it is plain regression.

**Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)** is a linear model with a continuous outcome, at least one continuous predictor (the covariate), and at least one categorical predictor (the factor). ANCOVA is built directly on the regression equation from @sec-regression. A simple linear model is

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$$

Here $\beta_0$ is the intercept, $\beta_1$ is the slope, and $\varepsilon$ is the error. The model describes a single line.

ANCOVA adds a categorical factor to that equation. The chapter asks whether every group follows the same line, whether the groups share a slope but need different intercepts, or whether each group needs its own slope.

We answer these questions in order. First, check that the model explains anything at all. Then test whether the groups have different slopes. Only if the slopes are parallel, test whether the groups differ in adjusted means. Step 2 below defines adjusted means, the group means you would expect if both groups had the same average covariate value.

@tbl-11designs places ANCOVA beside regression and the two kinds of ANOVA from Chapters [-@sec-anova] to [-@sec-factorial-anova], each written as a model.

| Design | Predictors | Model | First question |
|:----------|:----------------|:---------------|:-------------------|
| Regression (@sec-regression) | One continuous | $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$ | Is the slope zero? |
| One-way ANOVA (@sec-anova) | One categorical factor (three or more groups) | One mean per group | Are all the group means equal? |
| Factorial ANOVA (@sec-factorial-anova) | Two categorical factors, fully crossed | Main effect of A + main effect of B + A × B interaction | Does the effect of one factor depend on the level of the other? |
| ANCOVA | One categorical factor and one continuous covariate | Covariate + group + covariate × group interaction | After the whole-model check, do the groups share a slope? |

: Four designs as linear models. {#tbl-11designs}

## Why adjust for anything?

Adjusting for a variable means comparing groups at the same value of that variable. **Simpson's paradox** is a pattern in combined data that reverses once the data are split into meaningful groups. It shows what can go wrong without adjusting.

The case fatality rate (CFR) is the percentage of confirmed cases that ended in death. During the COVID-19 pandemic, early data showed that Italy's overall case fatality rate was higher than China's. But once researchers split the cases by age group, the trend flipped. In every age group except the youngest, where neither country recorded a death, the fatality rate was higher in China. The apparent contradiction was explained by differences in the age distribution of cases [@vonkugelgen2021].

The numbers below are the ones that study compared. China's cases and deaths by age are as reported on February 17, 2020, and Italy's are as reported on March 9, 2020.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11simpson-overall
#| fig-cap: "Crude case fatality rates. Italy appears to have a higher fatality rate than China when all cases are combined."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of the crude case fatality rate with all ages combined. Italy's bar, labeled 4.4 percent, is nearly twice as tall as China's, labeled 2.3 percent."
age_levels <- c("0–9","10–19","20–29","30–39","40–49","50–59","60–69","70–79","80+")

dat <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Country, ~Age,    ~Cases, ~Deaths,
  "Italy",  "0–9",       43,       0,
  "Italy",  "10–19",     85,       0,
  "Italy",  "20–29",    296,       0,
  "Italy",  "30–39",    470,       0,
  "Italy",  "40–49",    891,       1,
  "Italy",  "50–59",   1453,       3,
  "Italy",  "60–69",   1471,      37,
  "Italy",  "70–79",   1785,     114,
  "Italy",  "80+",     1532,     202,

  "China",  "0–9",      416,       0,
  "China",  "10–19",    549,       1,
  "China",  "20–29",   3619,       7,
  "China",  "30–39",   7600,      18,
  "China",  "40–49",   8571,      38,
  "China",  "50–59",  10008,     130,
  "China",  "60–69",   8583,     309,
  "China",  "70–79",   3918,     312,
  "China",  "80+",     1408,     208
) %>%
  mutate(
    Age = factor(Age, levels = age_levels),
    CFR_band_pct = round(100 * Deaths / Cases, 1)
  )

fig1_df <- dat %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  summarise(
    Cases = sum(Cases),
    Deaths = sum(Deaths),
    CFR_crude_pct = 100 * Deaths / Cases
  )

ggplot(fig1_df, aes(x = Country, y = CFR_crude_pct, fill = Country)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", CFR_crude_pct)),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 4.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(y = "Fatality rate (%)", x = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

In @fig-11simpson-overall, Italy looks worse at face value, with `r sprintf("%.1f", fig1_df$CFR_crude_pct[fig1_df$Country == "Italy"])`% of its cases fatal against `r sprintf("%.1f", fig1_df$CFR_crude_pct[fig1_df$Country == "China"])`% of China's. But the two countries' cases might differ in age, and age matters because older people are much more likely to die from COVID than younger people. In these numbers, `r dat$CFR_band_pct[dat$Country == "Italy" & dat$Age == "80+"]`% of Italy's cases aged 80 and over died, against none of the `r dat$Cases[dat$Country == "Italy" & dat$Age == "0–9"]` cases under 10. So we split cases into 10-year age bands (@fig-11simpson-by-age). Within every band where anyone died, China's bar is taller than Italy's.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11simpson-by-age
#| fig-cap: "Fatality rates by age group. In every age band where anyone died, China's CFR exceeds Italy's."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart of fatality rate by 10-year age band for China and Italy. Rates climb steeply with age in both countries, from zero in the youngest band to 14.8 percent for China and 13.2 percent for Italy at 80 and over, and China's bar is taller than Italy's in every band from 10 to 19 upward."

fig2_df <- dat %>%
  select(Country, Age, CFR_band_pct)

ggplot(fig2_df, aes(x = Age, y = CFR_band_pct, fill = Country)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age band", y = "Fatality rate (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11simpsonrates
#| tbl-cap: "Fatality rate (%) by age band. China's rate is higher in every band except 0–9, where neither country recorded a death. Several bands under 50 are too small to see in @fig-11simpson-by-age."

rate_tbl <- tidyr::pivot_wider(dat[, c("Age", "Country", "CFR_band_pct")],
                               names_from = Country, values_from = CFR_band_pct)
knitr::kable(rate_tbl[, c("Age", "Italy", "China")], col.names = c("Age band", "Italy", "China"))
```

@tbl-11simpsonrates lists the rates themselves. The reversal happens because Italy's cases were older on average and China's were younger (@fig-11age-distributions). A country's overall fatality rate is an average of its age-band rates, weighted by the share of that country's cases in each band. Italy had a larger share of its cases in the oldest bands, where fatality rates are highest, so its overall rate is pulled up. China had a larger share of its cases in the younger bands, where fatality rates are low, so its overall rate is pulled down. Combining all ages without adjusting for age reversed the pattern within the age bands. Age is a confounding variable (@sec-2confound). The two countries' cases differ in age, and age drives whether a case is fatal. @tbl-11weighted shows the weighting band by band.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11weighted
#| tbl-cap: "Each country's share of cases and fatality rate in each age band (%). A country's overall rate is the sum of share × rate across the bands, so Italy's older case mix pulls its overall rate up."

wt <- dat %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(Share = 100 * Cases / sum(Cases), Rate = 100 * Deaths / Cases) %>%
  ungroup()
wide <- tidyr::pivot_wider(wt[, c("Age", "Country", "Share", "Rate")],
                           names_from = Country, values_from = c(Share, Rate))
tot <- fig1_df$CFR_crude_pct
names(tot) <- fig1_df$Country
wide_out <- data.frame(
  Age = c(as.character(wide$Age), "Overall"),
  Italy_share = c(sprintf("%.1f", wide$Share_Italy), "100"),
  Italy_rate  = c(sprintf("%.1f", wide$Rate_Italy), sprintf("%.1f", tot["Italy"])),
  China_share = c(sprintf("%.1f", wide$Share_China), "100"),
  China_rate  = c(sprintf("%.1f", wide$Rate_China), sprintf("%.1f", tot["China"]))
)
knitr::kable(wide_out, col.names = c("Age band", "Italy share of cases", "Italy rate", "China share of cases", "China rate"),
             align = "lrrrr")
# Each country's rates weighted by the other country's age mix
italy_on_china <- sum(wide$Rate_Italy * wide$Share_China) / 100
china_on_italy <- sum(wide$Rate_China * wide$Share_Italy) / 100
```

Swapping the age mixes shows how much the weighting matters. Italy's band rates, weighted by China's younger case mix, give an overall rate of `r sprintf("%.1f", italy_on_china)`%. China's band rates, weighted by Italy's older case mix, give `r sprintf("%.1f", china_on_italy)`%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11age-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Case age distribution by country. Italy's cases are older on average, and China's are younger."
#| fig-alt: "Two bar charts side by side showing each country's share of cases in each 10-year age band. China's cases are concentrated between 30 and 69, peaking at 50 to 59, while Italy's are concentrated from 50 upward, peaking at 70 to 79, with almost one in five cases at 80 and over."

fig3_df <- dat %>%
  group_by(Country, Age) %>%
  summarise(Cases = sum(Cases), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(Prop = Cases / sum(Cases))


ggplot(fig3_df, aes(x = Age, y = Prop, fill = Country, group=Country)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~Country)+
  labs(x = "Age band", y = "Share of cases", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1))
```

This kind of reversal happens when the groups differ in their mix of a third variable, here age. Once you compare within each level of the third variable, here within each age band, the within-group pattern shows up again.

ANCOVA handles this situation when the third variable is continuous, instead of grouped into categories like the age bands above. It compares groups at the same covariate value, so a difference between the groups on that covariate does not distort the comparison.

## Covariates and fixed factors

A **covariate** is a continuous predictor that is related to the outcome and helps explain part of its variation. In environmental studies, common covariates include temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, and pollution concentration. Including one removes the variation it explains from the error term, so the group difference is tested against less noise.

A **fixed factor** is a categorical predictor whose levels the researcher chose on purpose, such as urban vs. rural or shaded vs. open canopy. A **random factor** is a categorical predictor whose levels are a sample from a larger population of possible levels. For example, if your streams are in ten counties, county could be a random factor. You aren't interested in those ten counties for their own sake. They represent a larger population of counties, and you want your conclusions to apply beyond the ones you sampled.

Every categorical predictor in this chapter is a fixed factor. The distinction between fixed and random factors matters once you build mixed-effects models, which contain both kinds of factor. This course does not cover them. Mixed-effects models are a different idea from the mixed design (@sec-10mixed), which mixes between-subjects and within-subjects factors.

## What ANCOVA is

ANCOVA asks whether a *relationship* holds up across groups. That framing fits environmental work particularly well, because you usually can't experimentally strip out a covariate like temperature, rainfall, or season anyway. Often you wouldn't want to. It may be the reason you designed the study in the first place. In this chapter's main example, the covariate's relationship with the outcome is the question, and the interaction is the result you are testing for.

::: {.callout-note title="Note: ANCOVA with a nuisance covariate"}
Elsewhere the covariate is a nuisance instead, a variable you adjust for so a group comparison is fair (the second example at the end of this chapter). In that version, you test the interaction to check whether the slopes can be treated as parallel before comparing the groups.

A classic version from psychology compares anxiety scores across two therapy groups after treatment, adjusting for pre-treatment scores.

Both versions use the same test and the same math. They differ only in which term you came to interpret, so decide that before you fit anything.
:::

For ANCOVA, you need:

1)  A continuous dependent variable (the outcome)
2)  At least one continuous independent variable (covariate)
3)  At least one categorical independent variable (a fixed factor, in this course)

### Separate lines and parallel lines

::: {.fa26-skip}
Before reading coefficients off an ANCOVA table, it helps to see how one equation can represent two groups at once.

An **indicator variable** is a variable that equals 1 for observations in one group and 0 for all other observations. Categorical predictors get into a linear model as indicator variables (you'll also see them called dummy variables). For a factor with $k$ groups you include $k-1$ indicators. The group left out needs no indicator of its own, because an observation with 0 on every indicator must belong to it. That group is the **reference group**, and every coefficient involving the factor is interpreted relative to it. With two groups, one indicator does the whole job:

$$G = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{group 1 (the reference group)} \\ 1 & \text{group 2} \end{cases}$$

In R, `lm(y ~ x + Group)` creates these indicators for you automatically.

**An indicator can change the intercept, the slope, or both.** When an indicator variable is turned on (set to 1), it activates the terms multiplied by that variable. Where the indicator appears in the model decides which of these changes.

Consider two predictors: a continuous variable $x$ and an indicator $G$ (0 or 1). The numbers below are arbitrary, chosen to make the arithmetic clean. The worked example later in this chapter plugs in fitted coefficients for air pollution and area type. Use this model:

$$y = 3 + 2x - 7G + 1(xG)$$

When $G = 0$ (indicator off), only the baseline terms are active:

$$y = 2x + 3 \qquad \text{slope} = 2, \ \text{intercept} = 3$$

When $G = 1$ (indicator on), the term $1(xG)$ becomes $1x$ and the term $-7G$ becomes $-7$. Adding them to the baseline terms and collecting the $x$ terms and the constants gives

$$\begin{aligned}
y &= (2x + 3) + (1x - 7) \\
&= (2 + 1)x + (3 - 7) \\
&= 3x - 4
\end{aligned}$$

so the slope is 3 and the intercept is $-4$.

Turning on the indicator adds +1 to the slope and −7 to the intercept. The one equation gives two different lines, and the value of the indicator decides which one applies.
:::

A linear model can give each group its own line. A group term lets the groups' intercepts differ, and a covariate × group interaction term lets their slopes differ. ANCOVA tests, in order, whether the slopes differ between groups (the interaction term) and, if they don't, whether the groups differ at the same covariate value (the group term).

In @sec-factorial-anova, an interaction meant that the effect of one factor depended on the level of the other. Here the interaction means that the effect of $x$, its slope, depends on the group.

::: {.fa26-skip}
**Naming the pieces.** Written in the general form, the same equation gives each coefficient a name and a meaning:

$$y = \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\text{reference intercept}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 x}_{\text{reference slope}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 G}_{\text{intercept shift}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 x G}_{\text{slope shift}} + \varepsilon$$

-   $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ describe the line for the reference group ($G=0$).
-   $\beta_2$ is how much the intercept moves for the other group.
-   $\beta_3$ is how much the slope changes for the other group. This is the interaction term.
:::

The **parallel-lines model** keeps the group term but leaves out the interaction, so the intercept can shift between groups but the slope cannot, and the two lines are parallel. When the slope difference is not significant, we use this simpler model instead of keeping the interaction term.

::: {.fa26-skip}
**How R names the four coefficients.** These are the four coefficients R reports for this model, and each one can be checked against a graph of the two group lines. For `lm(y ~ x * Group)`, where `Group` has levels A (the reference) and B, R names the rows `(Intercept)` for $\beta_0$, `x` for $\beta_1$, `GroupB` for $\beta_2$, and `x:GroupB` for $\beta_3$. The worked example below follows the same pattern: `(Intercept)`, `AirPollution`, `AreaTypeUrban`, and `AirPollution:AreaTypeUrban`.
:::

### The steps of an ANCOVA

**Model.** For one covariate ($x$) and one two-level group, the full model, `lm(y ~ x * Group)` in R, has four parts. An intercept and a slope describe the first group's line, a group term lets the second group's intercept differ, and a covariate × group interaction lets its slope differ.

@fig-11onevstwo shows the three possibilities this model can produce.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11onevstwo
#| fig-cap: "The question ANCOVA answers. Left: one line describes both groups. Middle: the groups need different intercepts but share a slope, so the lines are parallel. Right: the groups need different slopes, so the lines are not parallel and the gap between them depends on where you look."
#| fig-alt: "Three scatter plots, each with two colored groups of points. In the first, a single black line runs through both groups. In the second, two parallel lines sit at different heights. In the third, one line falls slightly and the other rises steeply, so the two lines cross near the middle of the covariate range."
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-asp: 0.45

# Fixed seed: the caption and alt text describe this particular draw
set.seed(11)
n  <- 30
x  <- runif(n * 2, 0, 10)
g  <- rep(c("Group A", "Group B"), each = n)
B  <- g == "Group B"

# Three scenarios, deliberately kept on a similar y range so the shared axis
# doesn't squash the first two panels.
y_same     <- 8 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(n * 2, 0, 0.9)
y_parallel <- 5 + 0.5 * x + ifelse(B, 5, 0) + rnorm(n * 2, 0, 0.9)
y_slopes   <- ifelse(B, 5 + 0.9 * x, 12 - 0.2 * x) + rnorm(n * 2, 0, 0.9)

lines_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(x, g, y = y_same,     panel = "One shared line"),
  data.frame(x, g, y = y_parallel, panel = "Parallel lines\n(same slope, different intercept)"),
  data.frame(x, g, y = y_slopes,   panel = "Different slopes\n(an interaction)")
)
lines_df$panel <- factor(lines_df$panel, levels = unique(lines_df$panel))

one_panel <- levels(lines_df$panel)[1]

ggplot(lines_df, aes(x, y, color = g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.5) +
  # first panel: a single line fit to both groups together
  geom_smooth(data = subset(lines_df, panel == one_panel), aes(group = 1),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1, colour = "black") +
  # other panels: one line per group
  geom_smooth(data = subset(lines_df, panel != one_panel),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 5, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Covariate", y = "Outcome", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

ANCOVA works right to left across that figure. It first asks whether the rightmost panel is what we have (do the slopes differ?), and only if the answer is no does it ask whether we have the middle panel or the leftmost (are the parallel lines at different heights?).

**Step 0: Does the model explain anything?** Before looking at any single term, check the whole-model $F$-test. Like the $F$ ratio in @sec-8fratio, it compares the variation the model explains with the variation left in the residuals, here counting the covariate, the group, and their interaction together. It asks whether those three terms together explain more of $y$ than chance would.

-   **Null ($H_0$):** the covariate, the group, and their interaction together explain none of the variation in $y$.

-   **Alternative ($H_a$):** together they explain some of it.

R reports it on the last line of `summary(lm(...))`. If it is not significant, stop. The data give no evidence that the covariate, the group, or their interaction explains $y$, so do not interpret any single term.

**Step 1: Are slopes equal across groups?**

-   **Null ($H_{0,\text{int}}$):** parallel lines, the same slope in both groups.

-   **Alternative ($H_{a,\text{int}}$):** different slopes.

**If Step 1 rejects.** The slopes differ, so stop testing the group term. There is no single group difference to test, because the gap between the lines changes along the covariate. Describe each group's line instead. The model gives each group's slope, but it does not test whether each one differs from zero. To test each slope, fit a separate simple regression within each group.

**Step 2: Are adjusted means equal?** *(only if Step 1 did not reject $H_{0,\text{int}}$, so the slopes are treated as parallel)* Drop the interaction and refit the parallel-lines model, `lm(y ~ x + Group)` in R.

-   **Null ($H_{0,\text{group}}$):** no difference between the groups at the same covariate value, so the two parallel lines sit at the same height.

-   **Alternative ($H_{a,\text{group}}$):** the groups differ at the same covariate value, so the lines sit at different heights.

The **adjusted difference** is how much the groups differ when they are compared at the same covariate value. With parallel lines, it is the vertical gap between the two lines, the same at every value of $x$. R reports it in the group row of the parallel-lines model (`TypeRetrofitted` in the retrofit example below).

The **adjusted means** are the group means you would expect if both groups had the same average covariate value. To get them, evaluate each group's line at the overall mean of $x$. Raw group means compare the groups at whatever covariate values each group happens to have. Adjusted means compare them at one shared covariate value, the overall mean of $x$. So if one group happens to have higher covariate values, that difference does not enter the comparison. The second example at the end of this chapter works through one.

In the parallel-lines model, the covariate's coefficient is the common slope, the slope both lines share.

::: {.fa26-skip}
**Intercepts and centering.** Intercepts are evaluated at $x=0$. In the model with an interaction, the lines can have different slopes, so $\beta_2$ compares the groups at $x=0$ only, which may be far outside the data. **Centering** the covariate means subtracting its mean from every value, $\tilde x = x - \bar x$. After centering, $\tilde x = 0$ where $x = \bar x$, so the intercept and $\beta_2$ now describe the lines at the average covariate value. In the parallel-lines model the gap is the same everywhere, so centering changes the intercept but not $\beta_2$.
:::

**What to report.**

-   If the interaction is significant: "The effect of $x$ differs by group," then each group's line with its own slope test, and a figure with separate fitted lines.

-   If the interaction is not significant: the common slope and the adjusted difference (or the adjusted means), with a figure showing parallel lines.

As always, statistical significance doesn't guarantee ecological or practical importance. Interpret a rejected null in light of the study's design, measurement precision, and the size of the effect as well as its $p$-value.

::: {.callout-caution title="Warning: Two ways to misread an ANCOVA"}
-   Interpreting the group term when the interaction is significant. With different slopes, the gap between the groups changes along the covariate, so no single group difference or adjusted mean describes it.
-   Reading the covariate and group rows of the `aov()` table after a significant interaction. R fits those rows in sequence, so the covariate row is one average slope for both groups and the group row is a difference after that one slope, and neither describes groups whose slopes differ.
:::

### Checking ANCOVA's assumptions

One of these, normal residuals with similar variances across groups, is the same as ANOVA's. The other three are new because a covariate has entered the model (@tbl-11assumptions).

| Assumption | New with ANCOVA? | How to check |
|:----------------------------|:--------|:------------------------|
| Normal residuals and similar variances across groups | No (Sections [-@sec-8assumptions] and [-@sec-9assumptions]) | Residuals-versus-fitted plot, Levene's test, Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals |
| Linearity within each group | Yes | A scatter plot with a fitted line for each group |
| Homogeneity of slopes (the groups' lines are parallel) | Yes | The interaction test (Step 1), not a check run beforehand |
| The covariate is measured with little error and is not affected by the group factor (the treatment) | Yes | The study design |

: Assumptions of ANCOVA and how to check them. {#tbl-11assumptions}

If the covariate is measured with error, ANCOVA only partly adjusts for group differences in the covariate, and the leftover difference can look like a treatment effect. If the treatment changes the covariate, adjusting for the covariate removes part of the treatment's own effect, and the adjusted difference understates it.

@tbl-11card-ancova summarizes the three steps of an ANCOVA.

+:---------------+:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Purpose        | Does the covariate's relationship with the outcome differ between groups?                                                                |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | If not, do the groups differ at the same covariate value?                                                                                |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Hypotheses     | Step 0: $H_0$: the covariate, the group, and their interaction explain none of the variation in $y$.                                     |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | $H_a$: together they explain some of it.                                                                                                 |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Step 1: $H_{0,\text{int}}$: the two slopes are equal (parallel lines).                                                                   |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | $H_{a,\text{int}}$: the slopes differ.                                                                                                   |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Step 2, only if Step 1 fails to reject: $H_{0,\text{group}}$: in the parallel-lines model, the two lines sit at the same height.         |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | $H_{a,\text{group}}$: the lines sit at different heights.                                                                                |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Assumptions    | Normal residuals and similar variances across groups                                                                                     |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Linearity within each group                                                                                                              |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Homogeneity of slopes (tested in Step 1)                                                                                                 |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | A covariate measured with little error and not affected by the treatment                                                                 |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Test statistic | Step 0: whole-model $F(3, N-4)$, where $N$ is the total number of observations                                                           |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Step 1: $F(1, N-4)$ for the interaction row                                                                                              |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | Step 2: $t$ = adjusted difference / its $SE$, from the group row of the parallel-lines model, $df = N - 3$                               |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Report         | If the interaction is significant: its $F(df)$, $p$, model $R^2$, and each group's slope from a separate regression with $t(df)$ and $p$ |
|                |                                                                                                                                          |
|                | If not: the adjusted difference with $t(df)$, $p$ and 95% CI, the adjusted means, the common slope, and the interaction $F$              |
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Summary of ANCOVA. {#tbl-11card-ancova tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

@fig-11steps lays out the same steps as a decision path, with the example in this chapter that follows each branch.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11steps
#| fig-cap: "The order of the tests in an ANCOVA. Each step runs only if the step before it allows."
#| fig-alt: "Flow diagram of the ANCOVA steps. The top box, Step 0, asks whether the whole-model F is significant. A No arrow leads right to a box that says stop and interpret no single term. A Yes arrow leads down to Step 1, which asks whether the covariate by group interaction is significant. From Step 1, a Yes arrow leads down to a box that says the slopes differ, so describe each group's line and test each slope with its own regression, labeled bird example. A No arrow leads to Step 2, which says to refit the parallel-lines model, test the group term (the adjusted difference), and report the adjusted means, labeled retrofit example."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "100%"

# Boxes on a 0-10 by 0-10 canvas: centre (x, y), width w, height h
bx <- data.frame(
  id    = c("s0", "stop", "s1", "yes", "no"),
  x     = c(3.0, 8.45, 3.0, 2.45, 7.55),
  y     = c(8.8, 8.8, 5.9, 1.75, 1.75),
  w     = c(5.0, 2.9, 5.0, 4.7, 4.7),
  h     = c(1.6, 1.9, 1.9, 3.1, 3.1),
  title = c("Step 0", "Stop", "Step 1", "Slopes differ", "Step 2"),
  body  = c("Is the whole-model F significant?",
            "Interpret no\nsingle term.",
            "Is the covariate × group\ninteraction significant?",
            "Describe each group's line.\nTest each slope with its\nown regression.",
            "Refit the parallel-lines model.\nTest the group term\n(the adjusted difference).\nReport the adjusted means."),
  ex    = c(NA, NA, NA, "Bird example", "Retrofit example")
)
bx$top <- bx$y + bx$h / 2
bx$bot <- bx$y - bx$h / 2
bx$lft <- bx$x - bx$w / 2
bx$rgt <- bx$x + bx$w / 2
b <- split(bx, bx$id)
nlines <- function(z) lengths(strsplit(z, "\n"))
lh <- 0.42   # one line of text, in canvas units

arrows <- data.frame(
  x    = c(b$s0$rgt, b$s0$x,   b$yes$x,  b$s1$rgt, b$no$x),
  y    = c(b$s0$y,   b$s0$bot, b$s1$bot, b$s1$y,   b$s1$y),
  xend = c(b$stop$lft, b$s1$x, b$yes$x,  b$no$x,   b$no$x),
  yend = c(b$stop$y, b$s1$top, b$yes$top, b$s1$y,  b$no$top),
  head = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
arrow_labels <- data.frame(
  x     = c((b$s0$rgt + b$stop$lft) / 2, b$s0$x + 0.15, b$yes$x + 0.15, b$no$x + 0.15),
  y     = c(b$s0$y + 0.3, (b$s0$bot + b$s1$top) / 2, (b$s1$bot + b$yes$top) / 2,
            (b$s1$y + b$no$top) / 2),
  label = c("No", "Yes", "Yes", "No"),
  hjust = c(0.5, 0, 0, 0)
)

# Title sits at the top of each box's text block, body below it, example last
n_body <- nlines(bx$body)
n_all  <- 1 + n_body + ifelse(is.na(bx$ex), 0, 1)
bx$title_y <- bx$y + (n_all - 1) * lh / 2
bx$body_y  <- bx$title_y - lh * (1 + (n_body - 1) / 2)
bx$ex_y    <- bx$title_y - lh * (n_all - 1)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = bx, aes(xmin = lft, xmax = rgt, ymin = bot, ymax = top),
            fill = "grey95", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(data = subset(arrows, head), aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "in"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(data = subset(arrows, !head), aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = arrow_labels, aes(x, y, label = label, hjust = hjust),
            size = 3.88, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_text(data = bx, aes(x, title_y, label = title), size = 3.88, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(data = bx, aes(x, body_y, label = body), size = 3.88, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = subset(bx, !is.na(ex)), aes(x, ex_y, label = ex),
            size = 3.88, fontface = "italic", colour = "grey30") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()
```

## Full ANCOVA example

### Birds, air pollution and area type

Suppose we are studying the effect of air pollution, measured as PM2.5 (fine particulate matter, in µg/m³), on bird density, in birds per hectare, and we want to know whether that relationship differs between urban and rural areas. @fig-11design lays out the design.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11design
#| fig-cap: "An ANCOVA design: one continuous predictor and one categorical factor."
#| fig-alt: "Study design schematic. Two predictors: area type with levels Rural and Urban, crossed with air pollution as a continuous gradient from low to high, across 200 observations. DV: bird density, in birds per hectare."
#| fig-asp: 0.36
#| out-width: "100%"

design_mixed("PM2.5 (continuous) × Area type (categorical)",
             "low", "high", "200 observations", c("Rural", "Urban"),
             "Bird density (birds per hectare)",
             "Does the pollution–density relationship differ between rural and urban?",
             note = "full pollution range measured in BOTH groups")
```

This design has the same structure as the factorial design in @sec-factorial-anova. Both cross two predictors and ask whether one changes the effect of the other. The only difference is that factorial's second predictor has levels, while ANCOVA's is a continuous range.

Both groups span the full pollution range, so rural sites are not simply the clean ones. An adjusted comparison compares the groups at the same pollution level, and that only works where both groups have sites at that level. Without the overlap, each group's line would have to be extended past its own data, the extrapolation problem from @sec-9prediction.

We might expect pollution to have a stronger negative effect in urban areas. Urban habitat is already fragmented and offers birds fewer clean patches to retreat to, while rural areas have more intact habitat nearby.

In the ANCOVA model, area type is the group factor, and air pollution is the covariate.

### Null and alternative hypotheses in our example ANCOVA

First, we state the hypotheses for each step:

0.  **Whole model.** Do air pollution, area type, and their interaction together explain bird density?

    $H_0$: air pollution, area type, and their interaction together explain none of the variation in bird density.

    $H_a$: together they explain some of it.

1.  **Slopes (interaction).** Does air pollution affect bird density the same way at urban and rural sites?

    $H_{0,\text{int}}$: the pollution slope is the same at urban and rural sites (parallel lines).

    $H_{a,\text{int}}$: the slopes differ.

    A significant interaction means the slopes differ, and air pollution's relationship with bird density depends on area type.

2.  **Adjusted means (only if the slopes are parallel).** At the same level of air pollution, do urban and rural sites differ in bird density?

    $H_{0,\text{group}}$: at the same pollution level, urban and rural sites have the same mean bird density.

    $H_{a,\text{group}}$: at the same pollution level, their mean bird density differs.

### The data

The data in this example are invented. There are 200 sites, about half urban and half rural, with PM2.5 between 5 and 30 µg/m³. The true slope is $-0.25$ birds per hectare for each 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5 at rural sites and $-0.75$ at urban sites, plus random scatter, so the fitted slopes below come out near these values but not on them. In this draw the fitted urban slope is about twice the rural slope, though the true urban slope is three times as steep.

```{r}
# Fixed seed: the invented bird data, and every description of them below, depend on this draw
set.seed(123)

n <- 200                                                     # number of sites
area_type <- sample(c("Urban", "Rural"), n, replace = TRUE)  # randomly assign area type
air_pollution <- round(runif(n, min = 5, max = 30), 1)       # continuous covariate, PM2.5 in µg/m³
urban <- ifelse(area_type == "Urban", 1, 0)                  # 0/1 indicator

# Bird density declines with pollution everywhere, but more steeply in urban
# sites. That difference in slopes is the interaction we want the model to find.
bird_density <- 40 -
  0.25 * air_pollution -                # rural slope
  3    * urban -                        # urban intercept offset
  0.50 * air_pollution * urban +        # extra urban steepness (the interaction)
  rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 5)            # noise

bird_density <- round(pmax(bird_density, 0), 0)

data <- data.frame(AreaType = area_type, AirPollution = air_pollution, BirdDensity = bird_density)
```

Before fitting the model, look at the data. @fig-11birddensity shows the outcome, bird density, by area type, which gives a quick sense of whether urban and rural areas differ on average.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11birddensity
#| fig-cap: "Bird density by area type. Rural sites have higher bird density than urban ones."
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of bird density for rural and urban area types. The rural box is centered higher than the urban box, with overlapping ranges."

ggplot(data, aes(AreaType, BirdDensity)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = AreaType), show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Area type", y = "Bird density (birds per hectare)")
```

Bird density is higher at rural sites, with a median of `r median(data$BirdDensity[data$AreaType == "Rural"])` birds per hectare against `r median(data$BirdDensity[data$AreaType == "Urban"])` at urban sites, consistent with what we might expect ecologically.

Next, check the covariate. @fig-11airpollution compares air pollution at urban and rural sites. If the groups differed sharply in pollution, a raw comparison of bird density would mix the area-type difference with the pollution difference, as the age mix did in the COVID example. When the groups have similar pollution levels, that mixing is small.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11airpollution
#| fig-cap: "Air pollution by area type. The two groups look broadly similar, so there is no large covariate imbalance for the model to adjust away."
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of air pollution for rural and urban area types. The two boxes overlap substantially with similar centers."

ggplot(data, aes(AreaType, AirPollution)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = AreaType), show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Area type", y = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)")
```

Air pollution is similar at urban and rural sites (@fig-11airpollution). The medians are `r median(data$AirPollution[data$AreaType == "Rural"])` at rural sites and `r median(data$AirPollution[data$AreaType == "Urban"])` at urban sites, a small gap compared with the range of about 5 to 30 µg/m³. This plot doesn't test anything, but it tells us what to expect. Because pollution is similar in the two groups, a group difference in bird density is unlikely to come from a difference in pollution.

### Results of the ANCOVA model

**Fit the model.** This is the same `aov()` call we used for one-way and factorial ANOVA. Because `AirPollution` is numeric instead of a factor, `aov()` treats it as a continuous covariate, so R needs no separate ANCOVA function.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ancova <- aov(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11ancova
#| tbl-cap: "ANCOVA table for bird density."

ancova <- aov(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)
anova_kable(ancova)
```

```{r}
ancova_lm <- lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)
fstat <- summary(ancova_lm)$fstatistic
whole_p <- pf(fstat[1], fstat[2], fstat[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
int_row <- broom::tidy(ancova) |> filter(term == "AirPollution:AreaType")
```

The whole-model test comes from the same model fit with `lm()`. Its `summary()` reports the whole-model $F$ on the last line.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ancova_lm <- lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)
summary(ancova_lm)
```

**Step 0: the whole model.** `summary(lm())` reports $F(`r fstat[2]`, `r fstat[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", fstat[1])`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(whole_p)`$, with $R^2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)`$. The model explains more of the variation in bird density than chance would, so we continue.

**Step 1: the interaction.** The `AirPollution:AreaType` row of @tbl-11ancova tests $H_{0,\text{int}}$: $F(1, `r fstat[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", int_row$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(int_row$p.value)`$. We reject $H_{0,\text{int}}$, so the slopes are not parallel. Air pollution's relationship with bird density depends on area type, so we stop here and do not test adjusted means.

**What the other two rows are.** The table still has rows for `AirPollution` and `AreaType`, both with $p < 0.001$, so it is tempting to read them, but they don't answer this chapter's question. R builds these rows in sequence, which means each row tests its term after the terms listed above it have been fitted. `AirPollution` tests one average slope for all 200 sites, ignoring area type, and `AreaType` tests a group difference after that single slope is fitted. Once the interaction says the slopes differ, neither row describes the data. There is no single slope, and the group difference depends on where along the pollution gradient you look.

Because the rows are built in sequence, and mean pollution differs slightly between the groups (`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(data$AirPollution[data$AreaType == "Rural"]))` µg/m³ at rural sites and `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(data$AirPollution[data$AreaType == "Urban"]))` at urban sites), listing the terms in a different order would also change their sums of squares. With a covariate, the order matters whenever the groups' average covariate values differ, even when the groups are the same size.

::: {.fa26-skip}
**Reading the coefficients.**

The `lm()` fit from Step 0 also shows the regression coefficients directly, so we can see how each term contributes to predicting bird density.

```{r}
lm_tidy <- broom::tidy(ancova_lm)

knitr::kable(
  lm_tidy |>
    transmute(term, estimate = round(estimate, 3), std.error = round(std.error, 3),
              statistic = round(statistic, 2), p.value = fmt_p(p.value)),
  col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "SE", "t", "p"),
  caption = "Linear model coefficients"
)
```

R automatically converts the categorical `AreaType` variable into a 0/1 indicator, the same $G$ from the indicator-variable section earlier in this chapter. It picks one level (here, "Rural," alphabetically first) as the reference, and every coefficient involving `AreaType` is interpreted relative to that reference. That's why you see a coefficient called `AreaTypeUrban` but no separate `AreaTypeRural` term.

These coefficients give the *direction* and *magnitude* of each effect:

-   **`(Intercept)`.** Estimated mean bird density for rural sites (the reference group) when air pollution is zero.
-   **`AirPollution`.** Slope of the relationship between pollution and bird density in rural sites. This is not the same quantity as the `AirPollution` row of the ANOVA table above, which was one average slope for both groups.
-   **`AreaTypeUrban`.** Difference in intercept between urban and rural areas, which compares the groups at air pollution = 0.
-   **`AirPollution:AreaTypeUrban`.** Difference in slope between urban and rural areas (the interaction).
:::

**Visualize the interaction.**

A scatter plot with fitted regression lines (@fig-11ancovalines) lets us see how air pollution relates to bird density for each area type.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11ancovalines
#| fig-cap: "Bird density against air pollution, with a separate fitted line for each area type. Both lines slope down, but the urban line falls about twice as steeply."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of bird density against air pollution, colored by area type, with separate straight fitted lines for rural and urban sites. Both slope downward, and the urban line is noticeably steeper, so the two lines diverge as pollution increases."

ggplot(data, aes(AirPollution, BirdDensity, color = AreaType)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "PM2.5 (µg/m³)", y = "Bird density (birds per hectare)", color = "Area type")
```

The two fitted lines have different slopes, which is the interaction the test detected. Both lines slope downward, so pollution is associated with fewer birds in both settings, but the urban line drops roughly twice as fast. The lines are about `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(coef(ancova_lm)[3] + coef(ancova_lm)[4]*min(data$AirPollution)))` birds per hectare apart at the lowest pollution levels and about `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(coef(ancova_lm)[3] + coef(ancova_lm)[4]*max(data$AirPollution)))` apart at the highest. @tbl-11gap reads the gap off the two lines at three pollution levels. Because the gap grows with pollution, no single group difference describes these data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11gap
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted bird density (birds per hectare) from each area type's own fitted line at the lowest, average and highest pollution. The gap between urban and rural sites grows with pollution."

px <- c(min(data$AirPollution), mean(data$AirPollution), max(data$AirPollution))
pr <- predict(ancova_lm, newdata = data.frame(AirPollution = rep(px, 2),
                                              AreaType = rep(c("Rural", "Urban"), each = 3)))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    pm = sprintf("%.1f", px),
    Rural = sprintf("%.1f", pr[1:3]),
    Urban = sprintf("%.1f", pr[4:6]),
    Gap = sprintf("%.1f", pr[4:6] - pr[1:3])
  ),
  col.names = c("PM2.5 (µg/m³)", "Rural", "Urban", "Urban minus rural"),
  align = "rrrr"
)
```

**Testing each group's slope.** The interaction told us the two slopes differ from each other. It did not tell us whether each one differs from zero, so we fit a separate simple regression within each group.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution, data = subset(data, AreaType == "Rural"))
lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution, data = subset(data, AreaType == "Urban"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11slopes
#| tbl-cap: "Separate regressions of bird density on air pollution within each area type."

slopes_raw <- data |>
  group_by(AreaType) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    fit <- lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution, data = .x)
    broom::tidy(fit) |> mutate(df = fit$df.residual)
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(term == "AirPollution")
sl_rur <- slopes_raw[slopes_raw$AreaType == "Rural", ]
sl_urb <- slopes_raw[slopes_raw$AreaType == "Urban", ]

slopes_tbl <- slopes_raw |>
  transmute(`Area type` = AreaType, Slope = round(estimate, 3), SE = round(std.error, 3),
            t = round(statistic, 2), df, p = fmt_p(p.value))
knitr::kable(slopes_tbl)
```

Both slopes are significant. Bird density falls with pollution at rural sites and falls about twice as steeply at urban sites. These are the same two slopes the ANCOVA model fit, because a model with an interaction fits each group its own line. Only the tests are new, and their standard errors differ slightly because each regression estimates its own error variance.

::: {.fa26-skip}
In the coefficient table, the rural slope is the `AirPollution` coefficient, $`r sprintf('%.3f', coef(ancova_lm)[2])`$, and the urban slope is $`r sprintf('%.3f', coef(ancova_lm)[2])` + (`r sprintf('%.3f', coef(ancova_lm)[4])`) \approx `r sprintf('%.3f', coef(ancova_lm)[2] + coef(ancova_lm)[4])`$.
:::

The points scatter around each line. The model's $R^2$ is `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)`, so air pollution, area type, and their interaction explain about `r round(100*summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)`% of the variation in bird density. The remaining `r 100 - round(100*summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)`% is the random scatter built into these invented data. In field data, that remainder would include other factors, measurement noise, and natural variability. An $R^2$ of `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)` is large partly because the data were invented to illustrate the method.

::: {.fa26-skip}
**Centering the covariate.**

Interpreting intercepts at $x = 0$ can be misleading when "zero pollution" isn't meaningful.

By centering the covariate (subtracting its mean), we make the intercept the predicted bird density for rural sites at mean air pollution instead.

```{r}
data <- data |> mutate(AirPollution_c = AirPollution - mean(AirPollution))
fit_centered <- lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution_c * AreaType, data = data)

tidy_centered <- broom::tidy(fit_centered) |>
  transmute(term, estimate = round(estimate, 3), p.value = fmt_p(p.value))
cc <- coef(fit_centered)

knitr::kable(
  tidy_centered,
  col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "p"),
  caption = "Coefficients with the covariate centered"
)
```

Centering doesn't change the slopes, the interaction, or their $p$-values. It moves the intercept and the group term, and the group term's test now compares the groups at average pollution instead of at zero, so its $p$-value changes too.

**Interpreting the centered model.** The mean pollution level is about `r round(mean(data$AirPollution))` µg/m³.

-   **Intercept (`r sprintf("%.1f", cc["(Intercept)"])`).** Predicted bird density for rural sites at average air pollution.

-   **`AreaTypeUrban` ($`r sprintf("%.1f", cc["AreaTypeUrban"])`$).** At the mean pollution level, urban sites have about `r round(abs(cc["AreaTypeUrban"]))` fewer birds than rural sites.

-   **`AirPollution_c` ($`r sprintf("%.3f", cc["AirPollution_c"])`$).** Slope for rural sites: bird density falls by about `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(cc["AirPollution_c"]))` birds per hectare for each additional 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5.

-   **Interaction ($`r sprintf("%.3f", cc["AirPollution_c:AreaTypeUrban"])`$).** Difference in slopes between groups. The urban slope = $`r sprintf("%.3f", cc["AirPollution_c"])` + (`r sprintf("%.3f", cc["AirPollution_c:AreaTypeUrban"])`) \approx `r sprintf("%.3f", cc["AirPollution_c"] + cc["AirPollution_c:AreaTypeUrban"])`$, roughly twice as steep a decline as in rural sites.

The group difference changed when we centered, from $`r sprintf("%.1f", coef(ancova_lm)["AreaTypeUrban"])`$ to $`r sprintf("%.1f", cc["AreaTypeUrban"])`$. Uncentered, the term compares groups at pollution = 0, a value outside the observed data. Centered, it compares them at average pollution, a value inside the observed range. When slopes differ, "the group difference" is not one number. It depends on where along the covariate you look.
:::

**Summarize and interpret.**

The significant interaction shows that air pollution's effect on bird density depends on area type. Bird density declines with pollution in both settings, but the decline is about twice as steep in urban sites. Because the interaction is significant, we focus on these different slopes, not on adjusted mean differences.

If the interaction had *not* been significant, we would instead drop the interaction term and interpret the parallel-lines model, comparing adjusted means between groups. The next example shows that case.

::: {.callout-important title="Results reporting: ANCOVA"}
> Results from the ANCOVA indicated that air pollution's effect on bird density depended on area type, $F(1, `r fstat[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", int_row$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(int_row$p.value)`$, model $R^2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(ancova_lm)$r.squared)`$. Separate regressions showed that bird density declined with increasing pollution at both rural sites, $b_1 = `r sprintf("%.2f", sl_rur$estimate)`$ birds per hectare for each 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5, $t(`r sl_rur$df`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", sl_rur$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(sl_rur$p.value)`$, and urban sites, $b_1 = `r sprintf("%.2f", sl_urb$estimate)`$, $t(`r sl_urb$df`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", sl_urb$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(sl_urb$p.value)`$, with the urban decline roughly twice as steep. These findings suggest that bird density declines more steeply with pollution in urban areas, which may call for area-specific conservation strategies.
:::

## Second example: when the covariate is a nuisance

In the bird example, the covariate relationship was the question, and the interaction was the finding. The other way you'll see ANCOVA reverses those roles. A **nuisance covariate** is a covariate you adjust for so that a group comparison is fair, when the group comparison is the question. This is also the continuous version of the Simpson's paradox problem the chapter opened with.

@tbl-11tworoles compares the two ways this chapter uses ANCOVA.

| Role of the covariate | The covariate is | What you interpret | Example in this chapter |
|:--------|:--------------|:--------------------|:------------------|
| Covariate as the question | The relationship you came to study | The interaction term, which tests whether the slopes differ | Air pollution and bird density, urban vs. rural sites |
| Nuisance covariate | Something to adjust for so the group comparison is fair | The group term, the adjusted difference, from the parallel-lines model | Occupancy and electricity use, retrofitted vs. standard buildings |

: Two roles for the covariate in ANCOVA. {#tbl-11tworoles}

### Retrofits and electricity use

A city facilities office wants to know whether energy retrofits (new insulation, lighting, and controls) reduced electricity use. It compares 30 retrofitted buildings with 30 standard ones. Electricity use depends heavily on how many people are in a building, and the retrofitted buildings happen to be the busier ones. These buildings are invented. In the invented data, a retrofit cuts electricity use by 40 kWh per day at any occupancy, both kinds of building use 2 more kWh per day for each extra occupant, and retrofitted buildings hold 60 to 120 people against 30 to 90 for standard ones.

Occupancy also passes the last check on the assumptions list. We treat average daily occupancy as measured with little error, and a retrofit changes a building's equipment, not how many people use it, so adjusting for occupancy doesn't remove any of the retrofit's own effect.

```{r}
# Fixed seed: the invented building data and the figure's alt text depend on this draw
set.seed(2)
n_b <- 30
occ_standard    <- runif(n_b, 30, 90)
occ_retrofitted <- runif(n_b, 60, 120)   # retrofitted buildings are busier

energy <- data.frame(
  Type      = factor(rep(c("Standard", "Retrofitted"), each = n_b),
                     levels = c("Standard", "Retrofitted")),
  Occupancy = round(c(occ_standard, occ_retrofitted))
)
# Same slope in both groups; retrofits lower use by 40 kWh/day at any occupancy
energy$Energy <- round(200 + 2 * energy$Occupancy -
                         40 * (energy$Type == "Retrofitted") +
                         rnorm(2 * n_b, 0, 20))

occ_means <- tapply(energy$Occupancy, energy$Type, mean)
raw_means <- tapply(energy$Energy, energy$Type, mean)
raw_t     <- t.test(Energy ~ Type, data = energy, var.equal = TRUE)
```

### The raw comparison

Average daily occupancy is `r round(occ_means["Retrofitted"], 1)` people in the retrofitted buildings and `r round(occ_means["Standard"], 1)` in the standard ones. @fig-11energyraw compares electricity use without adjusting for occupancy. Retrofitted buildings use more, `r sprintf("%.1f", raw_means["Retrofitted"])` vs. `r sprintf("%.1f", raw_means["Standard"])` kWh per day, and a pooled independent-samples $t$-test (@sec-6indep) calls that difference significant, $t(`r raw_t$parameter`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(raw_t$statistic))`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(raw_t$p.value)`$. Taken at face value, the retrofits made things worse.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11energyraw
#| fig-cap: "Daily electricity use by building type, ignoring occupancy. Diamonds mark the group means."
#| fig-alt: "Boxplots of daily electricity use for standard and retrofitted buildings. The retrofitted box sits higher, with a mean of about 342 kWh per day against about 318 for standard buildings."
#| out-width: "60%"
#| fig-asp: 0.8

ggplot(energy, aes(Type, Energy, fill = Type)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily electricity use (kWh)")
```

### The ANCOVA

```{r}
energy_full <- lm(Energy ~ Occupancy * Type, data = energy)
e_f   <- summary(energy_full)$fstatistic
e_fp  <- pf(e_f[1], e_f[2], e_f[3], lower.tail = FALSE)
e_int <- broom::tidy(aov(Energy ~ Occupancy * Type, data = energy)) |>
  filter(term == "Occupancy:Type")

energy_par <- lm(Energy ~ Occupancy + Type, data = energy)
e_par <- broom::tidy(energy_par, conf.int = TRUE)
b1  <- e_par$estimate[e_par$term == "Occupancy"]
b2  <- e_par$estimate[e_par$term == "TypeRetrofitted"]
b2r <- e_par[e_par$term == "TypeRetrofitted", ]

occ_bar  <- mean(energy$Occupancy)
adj_std  <- coef(energy_par)[1] + b1 * occ_bar
adj_retr <- adj_std + b2

# Rounded pieces for the adjusted-means display, so its arithmetic reproduces
e0 <- round(coef(energy_par)[1], 2)
e1 <- round(b1, 2)
e2 <- round(b2, 2)
xb <- round(occ_bar, 2)
adj_std_r  <- round(e0 + e1 * xb, 1)
adj_retr_r <- round(e0 + e2 + e1 * xb, 1)
```

**Step 0: the whole model.** $F(`r e_f[2]`, `r e_f[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", e_f[1])`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(e_fp)`$. The model explains more of the variation in electricity use than chance would, so we continue.

**Step 1: the interaction.** The `Occupancy:Type` row gives $F(1, `r e_f[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", e_int$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(e_int$p.value)`$. We fail to reject $H_{0,\text{int}}$, so we treat the slopes as parallel. Each additional occupant adds about the same amount of electricity in either kind of building. We drop the interaction and refit.

**Step 2: the adjusted difference.** @tbl-11energypar shows the parallel-lines model.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
lm(Energy ~ Occupancy + Type, data = energy)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11energypar
#| tbl-cap: "Parallel-lines model: electricity use on occupancy and building type."

knitr::kable(
  e_par |>
    transmute(term, estimate = round(estimate, 2), std.error = round(std.error, 2),
              statistic = round(statistic, 2), p.value = fmt_p(p.value)),
  col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "SE", "t", "p")
)
```

The `Occupancy` coefficient is the common slope, about `r sprintf("%.2f", b1)` kWh per day for each additional occupant. The `TypeRetrofitted` coefficient is the adjusted difference. At the same occupancy, retrofitted buildings use `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(b2))` kWh per day less than standard ones, $t(`r energy_par$df.residual`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", b2r$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(b2r$p.value)`$. The $t$ has `r energy_par$df.residual` degrees of freedom, `r nrow(energy)` buildings minus the 3 coefficients the model estimates. We reject $H_{0,\text{group}}$.

@fig-11energyadj shows what that coefficient measures. The adjusted means express the same comparison as one value for each building type. Evaluating each line at the overall mean occupancy, `r sprintf("%.2f", xb)` people, gives each building type's adjusted mean in kWh per day.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Standard:}\quad & `r sprintf("%.2f", e0)` + `r sprintf("%.2f", e1)`(`r sprintf("%.2f", xb)`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_std_r)` \\
\text{Retrofitted:}\quad & (`r sprintf("%.2f", e0)` - `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(e2))`) + `r sprintf("%.2f", e1)`(`r sprintf("%.2f", xb)`) = `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_retr_r)` \\
\text{Difference:}\quad & `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_retr_r)` - `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_std_r)` = `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_retr_r - adj_std_r)`
\end{aligned}$$

Their difference is the adjusted difference, the gap between the lines.

```{r}
#| label: fig-11energyadj
#| fig-cap: "Electricity use against occupancy, with the parallel lines from the model. Open circles mark the adjusted means, each line's value at the overall mean occupancy (dashed line). The arrow is the adjusted difference, which is the same at every occupancy."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of daily electricity use against average daily occupancy for standard and retrofitted buildings, with two parallel fitted lines. The retrofitted points sit further right, at higher occupancy, but their line sits about 42 kWh per day below the standard line. A dashed vertical line at the mean occupancy of about 76 people marks two open circles, one on each line, joined by a double-headed arrow."
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-asp: 0.6

lines_df <- data.frame(
  Type = factor(c("Standard", "Retrofitted"), levels = levels(energy$Type)),
  b0   = c(coef(energy_par)[1], coef(energy_par)[1] + b2),
  b1   = b1
)
adj_df <- data.frame(Type = lines_df$Type, x = occ_bar, y = c(adj_std, adj_retr))

ggplot(energy, aes(Occupancy, Energy, colour = Type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(data = lines_df, aes(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = Type), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = occ_bar, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = adj_df, aes(x, y), size = 3.5, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = occ_bar - 3, xend = occ_bar - 3, y = adj_std, yend = adj_retr,
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.08, "in"))) +
  annotate("label", x = occ_bar - 5, y = (adj_std + adj_retr) / 2, hjust = 1, size = 3.3,
           label = sprintf("adjusted difference\n%.1f kWh/day", b2)) +
  labs(x = "Average daily occupancy (people)", y = "Daily electricity use (kWh)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The raw comparison and the adjusted one point in opposite directions, for the same reason as in the COVID example. The groups differed in a third variable. The retrofitted buildings were busier, and busier buildings use more electricity. Compared at the same occupancy, retrofitted buildings use less electricity. @tbl-11rawadj sets the two comparisons side by side.

```{r}
mse_raw   <- anova(lm(Energy ~ Type, data = energy))["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
mse_ancova <- anova(energy_par)["Residuals", "Mean Sq"]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-11rawadj
#| tbl-cap: "Raw and adjusted comparisons of daily electricity use (kWh). The raw error mean square comes from a one-way ANOVA on building type."

raw_diff <- raw_means["Retrofitted"] - raw_means["Standard"]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Retrofitted mean", "Standard mean", "Retrofitted minus standard",
                 "Test", "Error mean square"),
    Raw = c(sprintf("%.1f", raw_means["Retrofitted"]), sprintf("%.1f", raw_means["Standard"]),
            sprintf("%+.1f", raw_diff),
            sprintf("$t(%.0f) = %.2f$, $p %s$", raw_t$parameter, -raw_t$statistic,
                    fmt_p_eq(raw_t$p.value)),
            sprintf("%.0f", mse_raw)),
    Adjusted = c(sprintf("%.1f", adj_retr), sprintf("%.1f", adj_std), sprintf("%+.1f", b2),
                 sprintf("$t(%.0f) = %.2f$, $p %s$", energy_par$df.residual, b2r$statistic,
                         fmt_p_eq(b2r$p.value)),
                 sprintf("%.0f", mse_ancova))
  ),
  col.names = c("", "Raw comparison", "Adjusted (parallel-lines model)"),
  align = "lrr"
)
```

Adjusting for occupancy also shrank the error term. Run as a one-way ANOVA on building type, the raw comparison has an error mean square of `r round(mse_raw)`. In the parallel-lines model it is `r round(mse_ancova)`. Much of the building-to-building variation in electricity use comes from occupancy, and once the model accounts for it, that variation no longer counts as error. Repeated-measures ANOVA gains power the same way in @sec-8rmanova. There the known source of variation was the units themselves (the monitoring stations), and here it is a measured covariate. Either way, removing it from $MS_\text{Error}$ makes the denominator of the test smaller, so a real group difference is easier to detect.

::: {.callout-important title="Results reporting: ANCOVA with parallel slopes"}
> After adjusting for occupancy, retrofitted buildings used `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(b2))` kWh per day less electricity than standard buildings, $t(`r energy_par$df.residual`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", b2r$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(b2r$p.value)`$, 95% CI for the reduction [`r sprintf("%.1f", -b2r$conf.high)`, `r sprintf("%.1f", -b2r$conf.low)`] kWh per day. Adjusted means at the average occupancy of `r round(occ_bar, 1)` people were `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_retr)` kWh per day for retrofitted buildings and `r sprintf("%.1f", adj_std)` for standard ones. The occupancy × building type interaction was not significant, $F(1, `r e_f[3]`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", e_int$statistic)`$, $p `r fmt_p_eq(e_int$p.value)`$, so a common slope was used (`r sprintf("%.2f", b1)` kWh per day per occupant).
:::

## Chapter Summary

**Why it matters.** An environmental relationship can differ from one setting to another. ANCOVA tests whether a continuous relationship, such as pollution's effect on bird density, is the same in every group. When it is, ANCOVA also compares the groups at the same covariate value.

**Core ideas**

-   **ANCOVA is regression plus a categorical factor.** It takes the familiar $y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\varepsilon$ line and lets a categorical grouping shift the intercept, the slope, or both.
-   **Check the whole model, then the interaction.** If the whole-model $F$ is not significant, stop. Otherwise test whether the groups' slopes differ ($H_{0,\text{int}}$: the slopes are equal). That answer decides how everything else gets interpreted.
-   **If the interaction is significant, report the two lines.** If slopes differ, describe how the relationship changes by group instead of reducing it to a single adjusted-mean comparison, which assumes parallel lines. Test each group's slope with its own regression, since the interaction only says the slopes differ from each other.
-   **If slopes are parallel, compare adjusted means.** Drop the interaction term and test the adjusted difference, the gap between the parallel lines. When the groups differ on the covariate, the adjusted comparison can point the opposite way from the raw one, as it did for the retrofitted buildings.
-   **A covariate also shrinks the error term.** Variation the covariate explains leaves the error mean square, which is the same way repeated-measures ANOVA gains power by removing unit-to-unit variation.
-   **The covariate must not be changed by the treatment.** If the treatment changes the covariate, adjusting for it removes part of the treatment's own effect. If the covariate is measured with error, ANCOVA only partly adjusts for it.
